name: Jamal Yilmaz

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Hi Jamal, thanks for doing this. I'm a field researcher with the Work Futures Panel. We're independent, with no ties to AI companies, employers, unions or political parties. Everything here is confidential, so you can tell me what you'd say in public and what you really think, and they don't have to match.

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: Sounds good. I like talking about this stuff, my wife says I never shut up about it.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Then let's start with your work. What does a normal day look like?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I'm on a timber-frame crew for a company that builds houses in panels. Half the week I'm in the factory on the edge of town, where the wall panels get made on a long line with a nailing machine, and half the week I'm on site putting them up with the crane. A good day is when a whole house goes from bare slab to roof trusses by four o'clock. A bad day is rain and a crane that won't start, and twelve of us standing in a container drinking bad coffee.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Where does AI come into your day, if at all?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: Every day, honestly. I use an AI app on my phone to read the panel drawings and flag clashes, like a window where a stud should be. I use it to plan my kids' lunches too, which my wife Dilan finds hilarious. She's a nurse on nights, so between us we've got Emre, who's eleven, and Ayla, who's seven, covered most days. We've got maybe four months' money saved, which feels okay but not great with the mortgage.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The first picture is called AI Plateau. Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say, well, it's still a useful tool, so let's use it properly. I'd keep showing the younger guys how to check drawings with it, because it catches mistakes before they cost us a day.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Quietly, I'd be a little disappointed. I like the stuff. But it'd also mean my job is safe and the factory keeps humming, so I can't complain too much.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep doing what I do and keep tinkering. I'd probably ask the factory manager, Lucy, if I can help set up the new scheduling system, since I already know the apps. Maybe that turns into a lead hand role and a bit more money.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calm, a bit flat. Like the big match turned out to be a nil-nil draw.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Tell me about a time the app caught something.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Two months ago we had a panel for a stairwell, and the app flagged that the opening was 50 millimetres short for the window that was ordered. I checked with a tape and it was right. That would have been a panel back to the factory and a day lost on site. Lucy bought me a coffee, which for Lucy is like a medal.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Is there anything about this world that bothers you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The pay, same as always. The company's got these machines making them more money each year, and our rates have barely moved. Even if AI is a flop, the gains from the factory line still mostly go upstairs. That's a fight for the union whatever happens.

S0.say: It's still a useful tool, so let's use it properly. I'd keep showing the younger guys how to check drawings with it, because it catches costly mistakes early.
S0.think: I'd be a little disappointed, because I like this stuff. But my job would be safe and the factory would keep humming, so I can't complain much.
S0.do: Keeps working and tinkering, and asks the factory manager to let him help set up the new scheduling system. Hopes this grows into a lead hand role with a pay rise.
S0.feel: Calm and a bit flat, like a big match ending in a nil-nil draw.
S0.quote: Lucy bought me a coffee, which for Lucy is like a medal.
S0.fieldNote: Jamal is an early, everyday AI user who sees himself as the crew's tech person. He'd be mildly let down by a plateau but secure in it. Even here his grievance is about how gains from machines are shared, which he sees as a union fight. He talks with energy and humour.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The second picture is called Steady Disruption. Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many tasks in many jobs. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. But most people still have work, and society has time to adjust. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say this is a chance, if we organise. The factory's going to get more robots, so the union needs to make sure the workers get trained to run them and get a share of what they save. I'd say that loud at work and online.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Between us, I think I'm in a good spot. I already know the tools, I'm in the factory half the week, I'm the guy people come to with their phones. It's the people who won't touch the stuff I worry about.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd ask the company to put me on the course for the new framing robot, the one they've been talking about buying. If they won't pay, I'd pay part myself out of savings, maybe 600, because it's an investment. I'd start learning how to programme the machine from videos at night.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Mostly calm, maybe excited. A bit guilty about being excited, if I'm honest.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Why guilty?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Because my mate Petar won't touch a phone app, and he's the best hand nailer I've ever seen. If the robot comes and I'm the one running it, it's partly his job I'm running. I'd want to drag him along, not leave him.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do for Petar?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Sit with him at lunch and show him one thing at a time. Not the whole app, just how to check a drawing. And push the union to get older guys trained first, not last. If we're smart about it, nobody needs to be left on the kerb.

S1.say: This is a chance if we organise. The union has to make sure workers get trained to run the factory robots and get a share of what they save.
S1.think: I think I'm in a good spot, because I already know the tools and people come to me with their phones. It's the people who won't touch any of it that I worry about.
S1.do: Asks the company to put him on the course for the new framing robot, and offers to pay around 600 himself if needed. Learns machine programming from videos at night and helps a reluctant workmate learn the drawing app at lunch.
S1.feel: Mostly calm and a bit excited, with some guilt about the excitement.
S1.quote: If the robot comes and I'm the one running it, it's partly his job I'm running.
S1.fieldNote: Jamal sees steady change as an opening and wants to move first. His progressive views show in his worry for less adaptable colleagues and his push for the union to train older workers first. He named the guilt himself without prompting. He would spend his own savings on training.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The third picture is called AGI by 2028. Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. With robots it reaches hands-on work too. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say we need emergency rules, and fast: a tax on companies replacing workers with machines, and the money going straight back to people. I'd be at the union meetings and arguing online every night, probably too much.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Off the record, even being the tech guy wouldn't save me here. If AI can do almost anything, it can run the framing robot too. My edge lasts a year, maybe. That's a strange feeling for someone who's always been ahead.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd use AI for everything I can to squeeze more out of the next two years, picking up weekend jobs quoting and drawing up small extensions for people, using the apps. Every extra bit goes into savings, aiming for a year of money instead of four months. I'd push the union hard for retraining money and a wage guarantee. And I'd vote for the party with the boldest plan, no hesitation.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious. Not panicked, because I'd have a plan and I'm good at moving. But there's a knot in my stomach.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What about Dilan's job?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: That's the thing that keeps me going, actually. Nurses on nights, holding someone's hand at three in the morning, I don't think people want a robot doing that first. So there's a chance her income keeps us steady while I find my feet. I hate putting it all on her, though.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said your edge lasts a year. What would you do with that year?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Earn as much as I can and learn the next thing before everyone else. Maybe the next thing is fixing the robots, maybe it's organising people. I'd rather be the guy explaining it to the crew than the guy hearing it from a letter.

S2.say: We need emergency rules fast, like a tax on companies that replace workers with machines, with the money going straight back to people. I'd be arguing for it at union meetings and online every night.
S2.think: Even being the tech guy wouldn't save me, because if AI can do almost anything it can run the framing robot too. My edge lasts a year, maybe.
S2.do: Takes on weekend quoting and drawing work for small extensions using AI apps, and pushes savings from four months toward a year. Presses the union for retraining money and a wage guarantee and votes for the party with the boldest plan.
S2.feel: Anxious, with a knot in his stomach, but not panicked because he has a plan.
S2.quote: My edge lasts a year, maybe. That's a strange feeling for someone who's always been ahead.
S2.fieldNote: This is the first picture where his tech advantage doesn't protect him, and he says so frankly. He counts on his wife's nursing job as a buffer but feels uneasy putting it all on her. He responds by moving fast and earning extra on the side. His politics turn sharper and more urgent.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The fourth picture is called AGI by 2031. Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any work a person can do, hands-on work included through robots. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say five years is enough to do this right if we start today. The union should be in every factory and on every site negotiating how the robots come in, not just reacting.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Five years is a gift for someone like me. I can ride the first wave, run the robots, and move into whatever comes next. I'd be 48, and I'd have more skills than I've got now, not fewer.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: First year, I'd get certified on the framing robot and the drone surveying gear, even if I paid for part of it. I'd go for a lead hand or line supervisor job in the factory. I'd talk to Dilan about putting money into a small business with a friend, doing robot-assisted extensions, while it's still early. And I'd run for union rep, because I think people trust me on this stuff.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy, but more excited than scared. The worry's more for others than for me.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Earlier you said even the tech guy wouldn't be safe. Doesn't that apply here too?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: It does, in the end. Five years just means I get some good years before the end, and I can build up savings and skills. I'm not saying I'd be fine forever. I'm saying I'd be fine for longer than most, and I'd use that to help people.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Which friend would you start the business with?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Kemal, he's a site electrician I've known since college. We've joked about it for years. With robots doing the heavy work, the two of us could do what used to take a crew of six. It's a bit cheeky to say that while I'm going on about protecting workers, I know.

S3.say: Five years is enough to do this right if we start today. The union should be in every factory and on every site negotiating how robots come in.
S3.think: Five years is a gift for someone like me, because I can ride the first wave and move on to whatever comes next. At 48 I'd have more skills, not fewer.
S3.do: Gets certified on the framing robot and drone surveying gear in the first year, paying part himself, and goes for a lead hand or line supervisor job. Explores starting a small robot-assisted extensions business with an electrician friend and stands for union rep.
S3.feel: Uneasy but more excited than scared, with most of his worry for others.
S3.quote: With robots doing the heavy work, the two of us could do what used to take a crew of six.
S3.fieldNote: Five years lets Jamal turn his early-adopter habits into a career move and maybe a business. He spotted the tension between his union talk and his plan to run a lean robot-assisted firm himself. He is honest that his safety would only be temporary. The time buffer clearly calms him.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The last picture is called AGI by 2036. Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any work a person can do, hands-on work included through robots. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say ten years is enough to rebuild how work is shared. Shorter weeks, public ownership of some of the big machines, proper retraining. I'd be pushing for it everywhere.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: For me, ten years means I can plan properly. I'd be 53, the kids would be grown or nearly. I'd have time to move into something like training others on the machines, or even teaching at the college.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd do the robot certificates, then a teaching qualification part time, so I can train apprentices on the new kit. I'd build up the side business slowly with Kemal, nothing risky. I'd vote and campaign for a shorter working week, because if machines do the work, people should get the time.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy, because the end point is still the same. But hopeful. Ten years is a lot of runway.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you tell Emre and Ayla?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: To learn how things work and how people work. Emre loves coding little games, Ayla wants to be a vet this week. I'd tell them both it's fine to change their minds five times, because the world will change its mind on them anyway.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Is there anything in the slow version that worries you more than the fast one?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Complacency. With ten years, people will say, ah, it's ages away, and the companies will quietly get everything set up their way. With two years everyone would be in the streets. With ten, I'd worry nobody pays attention until year eight.

S4.say: Ten years is enough to rebuild how work is shared, with shorter weeks, public ownership of some big machines and proper retraining. I'd push for it everywhere.
S4.think: Ten years means I can plan properly, and the kids would be grown or nearly. I'd have time to move into training people on the machines or teaching at the college.
S4.do: Takes robot certificates and then a part-time teaching qualification to train apprentices on new equipment. Grows the side business slowly with his friend and campaigns for a shorter working week.
S4.feel: Uneasy because the end point is the same, but hopeful about the long runway.
S4.quote: With two years everyone would be in the streets. With ten, I'd worry nobody pays attention until year eight.
S4.fieldNote: With a decade, Jamal shifts toward teaching and building slowly. His sharpest point was that a long warning invites complacency, and he worries more about politics than about himself. He stays uneasy rather than calm because he knows the end point doesn't change. His advice to his children is about flexibility.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: The 2028 one. I'm good at moving, but two years isn't enough for anyone to move far. What would help is paid retraining that starts now, not after, and a law that a share of what the robots save goes back to the workers they replaced.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: You didn't ask whether I'd want a robot on my crew. Honestly? Yes, for the heavy lifting. My back would love it. I just want it working for us, not instead of us.

headlineQuote: I just want it working for us, not instead of us.
portrait: Jamal is a 43-year-old timber-frame carpenter who splits his week between a panel factory and building sites, with a nurse wife, two children and about four months of savings. He uses AI every day and is the person his crew turns to with their phones. He stays calm through the mild pictures and moves fast to get trained on the new machines. In the fast AGI picture he admits his tech edge would barely last a year, and he grows anxious. With more warning time he plans robot certificates, a small business and teaching, while pushing the union to protect less adaptable workmates.
biggestWorry: AGI by 2028, because even someone who moves fast can't move far in two years.
whatWouldHelp: Paid retraining that starts now rather than after, and a law that a share of what robots save goes back to the workers they replaced.
